cosai:
- Ambiguous ownership is a growing liability for AI deployments; a formal shared-responsibility model is no longer optional
- AI-enabled systems exhibit probabilistic behaviors and novel risks (training data, user-generated content, model provider actions) unlike deterministic traditional software
- Traditional three-layer cloud shared-responsibility models do not address AI-specific concerns: regulatory accountability, training data governance, agentic boundaries, shadow AI
- The dependencies encoded in the five architecture layers remain invariant regardless of how an organization structures its teams
- Without layered accountability, the default outcome is a finger-pointing cycle where every party blames another
- Emerging agentic AI systems capable of semi-autonomous operation create accountability challenges beyond what prior frameworks addressed

- There must be exactly one accountable party per activity or component; overlapping accountability is not permitted
- Security and governance requirements must always cascade from the Business layer down through every supporting layer
- All autonomous agents must retain immediate human intervention capability, regardless of autonomy level
- Organizations deploying agents at autonomy level L3 or above must document their autonomy classification and review it quarterly
- At full autonomy (L5), organizations must require contractual accountability clauses from agentic providers covering cross-domain decision outcomes
- Model providers must always publish and maintain model version and vulnerability disclosures

- Exactly one accountable party per activity, the framework's core rule
- Five-layer enterprise architecture: AI Business & Usage, AI Information, AI Application, AI Platform, AI Model Provider
- Shared responsibility calibrated by operating model (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS), with customer responsibility rising toward infrastructure-layer deployments
- Responsibility shifts by autonomy level, moving from end user toward application developer and agentic provider as agent autonomy increases (adapted SAE J3016 L0-L5 scale)
- Complementary, not competing, with NIST AI RMF (what to do) and ISO 42001 (how to manage it); CoSAI SRF defines who is accountable
- Evidence-based accountability: an implementation playbook with evidence requirements per layer, not just stated principles
- Tiered human-intervention authority, a graduated response scale up to CISO/executive-authorized emergency shutdown

- Access Control
- Governance, Risk and Compliance
- Supply Chain
- Data Protection
- Log Management / Error Handling
- Threat Modeling
sans:
- v1.4 aligns SANS Critical AI Security Guidelines with OWASP AI Exchange so both use the same control taxonomy
- AI adoption is already embedded in enterprise products; blocking AI use is not a viable security control
- Public models, shared datasets, and third-party hosting create supply-chain paths for backdoors and poisoned artifacts
- Zero model trust: models cannot be fully trusted; external controls, validation, and guardrails are required at runtime
- Agentic systems chain tools and actions; scope creep without explicit constraints is a primary deployment risk

- Unauthenticated access to AI APIs or front-ends must not be allowed unless strictly necessary and monitored
- Augmentation data (system prompts, RAG context, vector DB content) must be treated as sensitive and access-controlled for read and write
- Sensitive data must be sanitized or anonymized before LLM incorporation; avoid commingling across trust boundaries
- Guardrails cannot be treated as infallible; high-stakes actions and irreversible agent calls require human oversight or escalation
- AIBOM disclosure must be restricted; technical supply-chain details aid adversaries if widely published

- Map controls to eight categories: Conventional Security, Data Minimization/Obfuscation, AI Supply Chain, Data/Model Engineering, Limit Model Behavior, Model I/O Handling, Monitoring, GRC
- Apply access controls to inference endpoints, model parameters, augmentation data, and training data using least privilege
- Vet public models manually; host approved models in an internal model garden; maintain AIBOM alongside SBOM practices
- Preprocess prompts and postprocess outputs; segregate user input from system context; rate-limit interactions
- Register models centrally; monitor inference, drift, and outputs; red-team and pen-test AI infrastructure on a schedule

- Access Control
- Data Protection
- Supply Chain
- Input Validation
- Vulnerability Management
- Log Management
- Secure Product Design
- Incident Response
